Header: 2025-03-18 15:00 UTC | Duration: 72 mins | Location: Zoom
Attendees: Priya Shah, Diego Alvarez, Evan Li, Sara Kim (Redwood) / Mark Holloway, Jin Park, Asha Patel, Tom Redd (Nimbus Labs)

[00:00] Priya Shah: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to spend today on runtime level stuff — kv cache patterns, batching, quant, and then the more complicated thing, MoE routing costs. who wants to kick off with priorities from Nimbus?
[00:12] Mark Holloway: yeah thanks, Priya. our main ask: stable p95 latency under 350 ms for 4k contexts at 50 qps sustained, and cost targets that don't blow up with MoE. we're also evaluating on-prem for regulated clients so VPC/or on prem constraints matter a lot.
[00:25] Jin Park: and we have a mix of workloads — short chatty prompts and some very long conversation histories, so kv cache effectiveness is huge.
[00:35] Diego Alvarez: great. quick note — we'll be using both Llama-3-ish and Mistral-style dense models and one MoE variant for routing tests. we'll talk about rope scaling too; long context drift shows up differently across architectures.
[00:50] [audio glitch] Speaker 2: ...sorry cut out...
[01:05] Priya Shah: ok Diego, can you explain how we model MoE token routing costs at per-token granularity? customers often see surprise cost spikes.
[01:20] Diego Alvarez: yes. two components: gating overhead and the expert execution. gating itself is small but non-zero — there's a dense matrix multiply to compute top-k routing and softmax, that increases latency per token. then the token is dispatched to selected expert shards; if experts are spread across GPUs you get cross-device comms and all the tail latency. so cost model = base dense cost + routing overhead + expert execution + cross-host comms.
[01:45] Tom Redd: when you say cross-host comms, is that Redis or NCCL allreduce?
[01:51] Evan Li: typically NCCL/infiniBand for activations; we limit cross-host by packing experts per device where possible. for on-prem you have to plan rack topology.
[02:05] Jin Park: any numbers? like how much does routing add on A100 vs H100?
[02:12] Diego Alvarez: quick ballpark from our bench: gating is ~0.1-0.5 us/token on H100, ~0.3-1.2 us/token on A100 depending on batch. Expert exec dominates — an expert forward for a 70B MoE shard could be roughly equivalent to 2-4 dense forward passes if not optimized, but with sharding and fused kernels we get down to ~1.1-1.8x. cross-host penalties can add 10-40% tail latency if not colocated.
[02:40] Mark Holloway: that matches what we saw in house; spikes when traffic shifts cause hot experts. do you have strategies for token affinity or routing smoothing?
[02:50] Sara Kim: yes — token affinity / capacity-aware gating helps. two patterns: preserve affinity by consistent hashing into experts for subsequent tokens, or soft routing with top-k temperature to smooth peaks. Redwood has routing policies to route by latency tier and throttle tokens when capacity approaches.
[03:10] [crosstalk] Jin Park: do you support dynamic shadowing or overflow to a dense fallback?
[03:15] Diego Alvarez: yes we do dynamic fallback to a compatible dense variant; that's part of graceful degradation. we can route overflow tokens to a lower-cost path or queue them, depends on SLOs.
[03:26] Priya Shah: switching to KV-cache — our concern: with 4k contexts and many parallel sessions, memory for KV grows fast. what caching strategies do you recommend?
[03:40] Diego Alvarez: three levers: prefix caching, sliding-window eviction, and per-customer TTLs. we also do compressed KV storage for older contexts (quantized KV) which reduces footprint but adds a decode cost on miss. balancing hit rate vs decode cost is key.
[03:57] Jin Park: how lossy is quantized KV? we've seen weird token generation drift when using int8 for kvs.
[04:05] Diego Alvarez: it's model and quant scheme dependent. NF4 style quant for activations is often better than straight int8 for KV because of distribution. but as you said, there's drift — especially for RoPE-scaling models where positional embeddings interact with cached keys.
[04:25] Tom Redd: tell us more about RoPE scaling — we've seen hallucinations after long prefix re-use.
[04:33] Sara Kim: short version: RoPE (rotary pos emb) relies on phase rotations; when you append extremely long sequences outside the range the model was tuned on, relative angles get weird — token alignment drifts, which looks like lower coherence or hallucination. fixes: linear RoPE scaling, ALiBi alternatives, or re-embedding recent tokens at a higher precision.
[04:55] Jin Park: is there a runtime trick to mitigate without re-training?
[05:00] Diego Alvarez: yes — we do periodic rebase of the KV cache: keep short-window high-precision cache for the most recent N tokens and compress older keys. Also clamp position embeddings when computing attention for cached entries — that reduces drift at some cost. We can auto-detect drift patterns via eval windows.
[05:20] [00:05:20.000] Mark Holloway: regarding batching, we want low p95 latency but high throughput for nightly bulk jobs. how does Redwood handle continuous batching vs strict fixed batching?
[05:35] Priya Shah: tradeoff — continuous batching groups requests opportunistically to improve utilization and reduce per-token cost, but it can add jitter to latency. fixed batching gives predictable latency but lower utilization. Redwood's scheduler exposes policies: latency-first (small max delay), throughput-first (up to 40ms assemble window), or adaptive where the scheduler learns target latencies and adjusts.
[05:58] Jin Park: any rules of thumb for assembly window sizes with H100 for 4k context?
[06:04] Diego Alvarez: for H100 at 4k, a 10-20 ms window usually captures enough requests to improve throughput without pushing p95 beyond target. for A100 you'd need slightly larger windows. But it depends on arrival patterns.
[06:20] Tom Redd: about quantization: we run validation sets — how often do you see regressions with int4 vs NF4?
[06:30] Sara Kim: NF4 tends to keep perplexity and human eval close to float16 for many open models; int4 often causes tokenization anomalies, especially with brittle prompts. We recommend a staged approach: NF4 for production, int4 for internal batch tasks where cost is critical and you can accept small quality loss. Always run eval suites.
[06:55] Jin Park: do you offer toolchains to measure quality impact?
[07:00] Diego Alvarez: yes — Redwood Optimize has eval hooks: delta-perplexity, embedding-ks tests, and token-level regression alerts. you can roll back quant in the rollout config.
[07:12] [07:12] Asha Patel: security question — if we move to on-prem how does KMS/HSM and audit logging integrate? we need key separation per-tenant.
[07:20] Evan Li: on-prem has customer-managed KMS and optional HSM integrations. audit logs are forwarded to your SIEM; we support per-token tracing and token-level cost attribution, but PII masking by default. we'll send the SOC2 whitepaper.
[07:35] Jin Park: one more on networking: we have constrained rack BW. how to prevent MoE spikes from overwhelming links?
[07:43] Diego Alvarez: architect experts to be local to inference devices that handle the same tenant traffic; use token throttling and soft-routing to limit cross-rack traffic; and for strict BW limits use batched dispatch with compression for activation transfers.
[08:00] [08:00] Mark Holloway: can you walk through a planned benchmark? we want apples-to-apples cost numbers.
[08:07] Priya Shah: yes — we'll propose a benchmark matrix: model variants (Llama-like dense 34B, Mistral-like 7B dense, 32B MoE), infra (A100 x4, H100 x4), contexts (128/1024/4096), batching windows (5/20/50 ms), and token arrival patterns (poisson bursts vs steady). we'll run p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, KV hit rates, cost per 1k tokens, and model quality deltas.
[08:40] Jin Park: please include a scenario where we deliberately hot-spot experts. we want to see failure modes.
[08:45] Diego Alvarez: yes we'll add hot-expert stress tests and fallback comparisons (queueing vs dense fallback).
[08:52] [08:52] Tom Redd: what's the recommended fallback latency target when an expert saturates?
[08:58] Sara Kim: generally keep fallback within 1.5x the p95 of normal path; if not possible, return degraded output with clear latency and dev flags so apps can decide.
[09:10] Priya Shah: we'll also run KV compression experiments — Diego, can you outline expected decode cost tradeoffs?
[09:18] Diego Alvarez: compressed KV (e.g., 4-bit per activation) reduces memory by ~2-4x but adds roughly 10-40% decode overhead on a miss. If hit rate is >80% for long-term context, compression wins. Otherwise keep hot window uncompressed.
[09:35] Jin Park: any gotchas with RoPE and compressed KV?
[09:40] Diego Alvarez: yes — compression artifacts can amplify RoPE drift for some models. that's why our suggested config uses high-precision for recent tokens and aggressive compression only on older prefixes.
[09:55] [09:55] Mark Holloway: how will Redwood measure drift? is there an automated detection?
[10:00] Evan Li: we run sliding window perplexity checks and embedding stability checks on a heldout prompt set; sudden deltas trigger alerts and can automatically switch to higher-precision KV for that session.
[10:15] Jin Park: what about runtime quantization switching — can Redwood switch a running model from NF4 to float16 mid-session if quality dips?
[10:24] Diego Alvarez: you can configure a session policy: immediate switch (requiring a short recompile) or route new tokens to a higher-precision fallback model while preserving older KV. both have tradeoffs: immediate switch costs time to reinitialize kernels; routing to fallback increases cross-model consistency risks.
[10:45] [10:45] Asha Patel: do you retain PII in KV? our compliance wants no raw PII in cached keys.
[10:52] Priya Shah: Redwood offers PII redaction and configurable retention TTLs; also you can disable KV caching per-tenant.
[11:05] [11:05] Tom Redd: ok final stuff — on-prem PoC timeline?
[11:10] Priya Shah: we propose kickoff week of 2025-03-31: infra sizing, runbench week 1, tune week 2, final report week 3. this lines up with Jin providing prompt sets.
[11:22] Jin Park: sounds good.
[11:25] [11:25] Priya Shah: recap of next steps — Priya will send perf sheet and security deck; Diego runs MoE sims; Jin sends traces; Asha asks for KMS docs. we'll schedule PoC kickoff. thanks everyone.
[11:40] [11:40] Meeting ends.
